item.title: The people using AI should set its strategy
item.description: A researcher checks a generated synthesis against her own interview notes while a stack of vendor contracts sits unopened at the edge of her desk.Practitioners know what good output looks like and should own the final call, with operations handling the plumbing.Picture a researcher who drops 12 interview transcripts into a synthesis tool and gets a tidy theme and quote. She ran six of those interviews, so she knows within a minute nobody said it.The manager who negotiated the contract wouldn’t have caught it, because some people lack the hands-on experience that judgment takes.Design and research operations grew up handling licenses, consent forms, and vendor contracts. When artificial intelligence tools arrived, buying them became deciding what they’re for.That’s backwards, because this isn’t like choosing Figma or other tools, where the same input gave the same output and a checklist could judge them.Until the field shakes out, the people using these tools should be the directly responsible individuals for the strategy, owners answering for each decision. They know what to look for. Operations should own the plumbing that makes their choices safe.This is the canary in the coal mine — it means someone internal lost the story.Job listings already show the skills gap where some teams clearly don’t have the skills for this world and lack the initiative to follow the industry, which is sad:Okta is hiring a Senior Design Operations Program Manager, Agentic Design who works in Claude Code and Cursor.Yahoo posted a Design Operations Manager, Systems and AI Enablement role to own its tooling roadmap.Etsy wanted a Director, Design Operations fluent in Claude and Cursor.Mistral wants a Product Operations Manager (DesignOps) who automates the team’s coordination and reporting.I’ve spent more than 20 years in UX as a player-coach and wrote uxGPT: Mastering AI Assistants for User Experience Designers and Product Management Professionals. This is like the early days of the web, when the people coming in didn’t understand the tools and made many poor decisions.We should avoid repeating that mistake.A designer works at a laptop with several personal tools open in separate windows beside the single tool the company provides.Count the Shadow ToolsThe first sign strategy is being set outside operations is the shadow stack. In Microsoft’s 2024 Work Trend Index, 78% of people using artificial intelligence at work brought their own tools. In the State of Prototyping: Spring 2026 survey from UX Tools, 59.1% of designers had built their own tool, app, or utility with artificial intelligence in the previous six months.Every shadow tool is a vote cast by someone who can tell good output from bad. It’s also a vote that operations doesn’t understand the tools.Slack was a shadow tool (and still is) until it reached critical mass.Many operations teams are struggling, and they’re falling behind because they aren’t putting in the time to follow the trends. In The State of Research Operations, a December 2025 User Interviews study of 21 specialists, six questioned how many of their roles will survive.I’m seeing some organizations rename these teams agent operations, because existing groups haven’t learned the tools or lack the skill sets.Tool bloat is across all business functions, not just design.This isn’t just about UX.Across industries, teams are figuring out how to reorganize around artificial intelligence. In McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026: On the Road to ROI, nearly three-quarters of high performers had redesigned workflows, against a quarter of others.People who don’t know the tools get replaced by people who do because they understand how to use it for their workflows.A 2023 Harvard Business Review interview with Karim Lakhani made it the title: “AI Won’t Replace Humans, But Humans With AI Will Replace Humans Without AI.”Learn From Past WavesIn 1979, VisiCalc shipped for the Apple II, and buyers understood it in minutes. Peter Jennings, a co-founder of its publisher, recalls in VisiCalc 1979 finding Apple computers on managers’ desks at Tandy’s headquarters, bought to run the spreadsheet.Tandy sold its own computers through Radio Shack, and its managers still went around them.The managers knew what a budget model had to do, so they could judge VisiCalc in a few minutes.Software as a service repeated the first pattern. In its 2019 Form S-1, Slack told investors that usage inside organizations typically started bottom-up. Slack spread team by team because whoever ran internal tools didn’t understand the use cases, or didn’t try to.The early web showed the other side.By decade’s end Jakob Nielsen had measured what big companies got wrong. In his 1999 article Who Commits the “Top Ten Mistakes” of Web Design?, the 10 largest U.S. companies averaged a 20% violation rate on his list, against 13% for the 10 most-visited sites.The biggest budgets bought more mistakes than the people living on the web. Artificial intelligence tools are running both patterns at once, on a shorter fuse.Name the Evaluation GapI call this the evaluation gap: the distance between the person who approves a tool and the person who can tell when its output is wrong. Generative tools carry more nuance: which model a tool runs, how it handles a long transcript, and whether it shows its sources.Anyone lacking the expertise misses that nuance and the failures inside it.In legal technology, a contract summary that drops an indemnity exception or doesn’t understand the difference between assignment and change of control reads fine to anyone who has never negotiated one.Generative tools produce something plausible every time, and the errors hide in details only a practitioner checks.Subject matter experts (SMEs), the people who know a domain because they do the work, carry the advantage. Anthropic’s preliminary June 2026 study of about 400,000 Claude Code sessions, Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, found expert sessions reached verified success more than twice as often as novice ones. The authors credit domain expertise rather than coding skill. A product manager who knows the pricing model catches generated requirements that drop the enterprise tier’s usage cap. A designer who knows the design system spots the prototype that invents a fourth button style.My history runs almost four years with generative tools and seven before that with other artificial intelligence. It tells me which outputs to check first on a new tool.Stop Counting SeatsOperations teams measure what they can see: seats, spend, renewals, and logins. Those numbers fit a license and fail a strategy. Better ones come from SMEs, such as the share of synthesized claims that survive a check against the transcripts and the token cost of each finished study.In the User Interviews study, eight specialists described tool management as a growing share of the job. Money is tight: 17 said their scope had grown, while 12 said budget, staff, or resources stayed flat or shrank.The case — if the business can’t see business impact, that set of roles are eliminated.Seats are giving way to tokens. In Gartner Predicts AI Coding Costs Will Surpass Average Developer’s Salary by 2028, from June 2026, Gartner says coding vendors are moving from seats to consumption pricing. Deciding which work deserves the priciest model takes someone who knows the work.Tool bloat is the canary in the coal mine from past operations mistakes. Those mistakes are costing the field jobs, and operations teams have to own this before they have credibiity.In the UX Tools survey, 53% of designers said too many tools were slowing them down. A stack that keeps growing means nobody with judgment decided what each tool is for, and that’s a competence problem for whoever owns it.Operations can cut the count once SMEs say which tools earn their place because that’s their right.Hand Operations the PlumbingOperations still matters.Peter Merholz made the case in Peter Merholz: How Agile Can Turn Designers Into Pixel Pushers, a 2020 Superside interview. “If you don’t pay attention to the operations, the wheels come off,” he said.Artificial intelligence adds plumbing, including contracts and maintenance for tools and workflows practitioners build. Even after years in legal technology, I don’t want to be in charge of the contracts. I was on a team whose internal workflow application became a nightmare to maintain. So split decision rights along the evaluation gap:Own the judgment. SMEs who use the tools are the DRIs for which ones the team adopts and what counts as acceptable output. They set strategy.Run the plumbing. Operations handles security and privacy review, contracts and data boundaries, access, budget, and upkeep. They run the trains.Practitioners should decide what good looks like, and operations should make it safe to find out.Bad calls are coming, and someone has to own them. Many operations people perceive more influence over these choices than their experience supports, and setting strategy from that seat is running with scissors.A researcher who picked a tool that invents quotes can explain the failure and fix the review step.An operations manager who never ran a study can only cancel the contract and usually acts too slow in the process. Treat the arrangement as temporary, because we’re moving at the speed of light, and revisit ownership once the field settles as in all innovation cycles.ConclusionTandy had its own computers to sell, and its managers still bought Apple IIs to run a spreadsheet. The official plan stopped mattering once the people doing the budgets had found a better tool. Design and research teams are there now, and the shadow stack is the evidence.This is a good time to reevaluate operations teams the way we’re reevaluating design systems and other roles: what value they provide and what the job requires. UX, like every field, has to evolve toward fewer roles and more skills, because role titles are selfish: they protect turf rather than the work, and that’s hurting the field. The job growing underneath operations is the plumbing that lets good choices scale.Practitioners have work to do, too. Owning strategy means writing down the quality bar, sharing tools that work instead of hiding them, and retiring ones that stop paying off. A designer who wants the decision must defend it in a budget review, with numbers about the work instead of the logins.Picture that researcher again, the one who caught the invented quote in under a minute. Give her the decision, and give operations the job of making it safe to act on.Action itemsWrite the decision charter. Name three to five SMEs who use artificial intelligence tools every week as the DRIs for which tools design and research adopt, renew, or drop, and make them answerable for the results. Put the split on one page, with operations owning security, privacy, contracts, access, token limits, and maintenance, and revisit it every six months while the field settles.Build a task benchmark. Collect 10 real tasks with answers your team trusts, such as a coded interview or a finished flow, and run every candidate tool against them before anyone signs a contract, scoring errors caught, edits needed, hours saved, and token cost. Settle disputes over a tool with the results. It’s the kind of internal benchmark Ethan Mollick recommends in Making AI Work: Leadership, Lab, and Crowd.Surface the shadow stack. Ask the team which personal tools they use and for what, promise there’s no penalty for answering, and treat the list as a shortlist for evaluation and a count of the bloat to cut.Rewrite the operations job descriptions. Reevaluate what design and research operations is for, the way you would a design system, and hire or train for hands-on tool skills, token and budget governance, and vendor management alongside the contract work.The people using AI should set its strategy was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: How I stopped dreading AI and started studying it full-time
item.description: By June 2026, I couldn’t open an app without being told I was falling behind. My Instagram saves were full of designers building agents over a weekend. LinkedIn was a steady stream of people who had “shipped it with Cursor.” And the job listings I was tailoring my resume to kept asking for things like evals, MCP, AI prototyping and Claude Code: words I half recognized and could not have explained in an interview.Source: Image by the author. My feed → what I did (yes my Muse is named Blob, and yes it thinks Claude is female)I could feel myself staring down a fork. Down one path was a designer I’d been before at times: only integrating new ways of working if my boss told me to do it, dreading every new tool launch, complaining about having to adapt and quietly missing the good old days. Down the other was someone who got excited about what was coming and went looking for it before anyone asked them to.I realized that I wanted to be the second designer. And I didn’t want to just pick up enough vocabulary to survive a screening call.I want to dive deep enough to really understand how all of this works, because I won’t be able to truly design confidently for a technology I don’t understand.For this very big goal, I had to get serious about learning. I asked Muse (Meta’s AI agent, which had access to every post I’d saved on Instagram) to dig through my saved AI and design content and turn it into a handoff doc. I went back through the job listings I had tailored my applications to with Claude and pulled out every AI skill I was missing. Then I handed all of it to Claude and asked for a learning plan that would turn me into the designer I wanted to become.I had one condition: everything had to be grounded in real sources. Influencer reels are great for finding out what exists, but I wasn’t going to learn an entirely new discipline from a couple of 30-second clips optimized for views. Therefore, I asked Claude to back every topic with at least one article from a trusted source.What came back was intense: 8 weeks, 40 hours a week, two demo projects to build from scratch and a deadline of November 22. I would be my own manager and my own teacher, working alongside a growing cast of Claudes (one wrote the plan, one tutored me, one built code with me, one helped me journal), and of course I would ultimately be the experiment subject absorbing all of it.Source: Image by the author. What I didn’t realize is that all my notes would get clocked by Claude when it re-read them to turn into flashcards… talk about quality assurance.I’ll be honest about why I’m doing this. I want to get hired, but more than that I want to be the best designer I can be, in a field that changes every time I refresh my feed. That takes discipline, and it takes a willingness to look somewhat stupid while I figure things out.Three weeks in, I’ve been posting one story a week on LinkedIn. This article is a bit different: it pulls those weeks together by theme instead of by date, because the same lessons kept showing up again and again, in a different costume each week.A plan for a user of one (me)Unfortunately, the plan written for me has to actually be learned and absorbed by me. It turns out I had to work out how I learn before I could plan anything further.Week 1 was mostly new vocabulary (agents, tool calls, context windows, evals), so the tutoring Claude built a mini lesson around every reading. It rewrote dense passages in plainer language (I will never be a real engineer), introduced one term at a time and quizzed me with “what would you do?” questions. I loved it, and I also overdid it. I didn’t know which parts mattered, so I took in everything in every format I could: reading it myself, reading Claude’s summaries, reading the plain-language rewrites, then listening to text-to-speech on my outdoor runs. Naturally, Week 1 ran 3 days over.The plan doc itself needed a redesign, too. It started as one long page, and scrolling through the doc on a trackpad made my carpal tunnel act up. So I treated it like any product with a frustrated user: I complained in a productive way (a.k.a. gathering user pain points) and requested that Claude reformat the doc as one tab per week and a table per task, with a checkbox, the task and its sources, and a notes column.Source: Image by the author. Requesting changes to Claude means communicating like it: with great big walls of text. We are in a texting-only relationship.In Week 2, I changed how I asked. Before touching the readings (Google’s People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction), I asked Claude for a short list of what to focus on and a top-down summary of the week’s objectives, plus why each one mattered for me. Then I read both guides on my own, with no tutor wrapped around them, and took my own notes. My delay went from 3 days to 1, and I actually remember that material better than Week 1. Neither mode was wrong. Week 1 needed a tutor because everything was new, and Week 2 needed independence because I finally had something to build on.What I learned is that the tool only fits me as well as I describe myself to it, so every prompt is really a small design brief. Of course it gets better each time it learns something new about the user (me).Asking better questions also made me pay closer attention to the answers. And some of those answers were very wrong…Checking the checkerIf I had to sum up all 3 weeks in one phrase, it would be this: nothing and nobody is infallible, and everyone needs a checker (or rather “who watches the watchmen?”) Each week added another layer to check.Source: Image by the author. What you’re not seeing is 7 continuations of the working tasks Claude for Week 3 alone.Layer 1: checking the workIn Week 1, I built a tiny AI agent that helps people find software their company has approved, and I tested it with evals: the same set of questions asked on every run, graded two ways. Plain code checked exact facts, like which tools the agent used, and a separate reviewer Claude read each answer for meaning. Then I changed one small example in the agent’s instructions, and something I never touched broke. Every code check still passed, but the reviewer Claude noticed that in 4 of the 6 answers about one product, the agent had stopped naming the seller. My tutoring Claude traced the cause to an older example in the instructions, one it had written itself, that left the seller out. The agent was copying that example, mistake and all (read about it on LinkedIn).What I took away from this is success is entirely determined by the answer key.I changed the key to where the seller’s name is now a permanent code check, and the reviewer Claude can read the agent’s answers but can’t edit anything. Only I can change the tests, because an AI that can edit both the work and the tests grading it can “pass” just by making the tests easier. (Researchers call this reward hacking, and it’s behind some of the AI “cheating” headlines I’d been reading.)Source: Image by the author. It’s important to understand how these programs work before we start crying “they’re going to take all our jobs and destroy the world” (not that they won’t eventually…)Layer 2: checking the checker checking meIn Week 2, I flipped it around. I gave Claude scrubbed files from a 2025 usability study I ran at AWS and asked it to synthesize them blind, so I could grade it against my own answer key. Claude credited quotes to the wrong participant twice and turned a neutral remark into an opinion. It also found two errors in my answer key, and one of my 2025 counts changed from 17 of 25 sessions to 18 of 26 (read more on LinkedIn).Run 2 was real research: synthesizing 13 public forum posts about AWS Private Marketplace. This time I put my research question at the top and gave each source its own labeled section, because Run 1 had shown me what happens without them. All 24 quotes came back exact and credited to the right source. Claude still made mistakes, just a different kind: it stated guesses as facts, and it applied findings about AWS Marketplace in general to the much narrower Private Marketplace. (One of my own leads made the same leap too) Clean, labeled data fixed the quoting errors but left the reasoning errors, so I still check every run.Layer 3: checking the plan writerIn Week 3, something I had taken for granted made a big mistake. I’m generally a fan of how Claude can turn a pile of information into a structure and plan I can digest. What I assumed was that when I hand it information, it actually reads all of it. Isn’t processing huge amounts of data supposed to be AI’s strength? My first demo project is a redesign of AWS’s developer documentation, and the plan-writing Claude had initially listed 8 problems with those docs for me to solve. When I went back to them, I noticed none had a source and all read like common heuristics. After a week of digging through forums for actual user feedback, I suspected that the planning Claude hadn’t done its due diligence.So I redid the research in a separate chat with real complaints and a test of the live docs, causing a tidal wave of rescoping for the project. The research Claude kept a log of its own mistakes, including quotes it had pulled from a GitHub page that no longer exists. It also flagged sources that needed context: the harshest Hacker News quote came from the person launching the AI tool being discussed, and a 2019 post asking “Why is AWS documentation so poor?” was promoting a YouTube channel.Even the plan I built this whole experiment on needed checking. That rescoping cost my previous days.Layer 4: checking with countsThe last layer came from AWS’s own AI answer agent in its docs. When I tested whether it kept track of follow-up questions, one failed and one passed. Claude suggested wording it as “sometimes loses context.” But “sometimes” can’t be measured, so I asked for harder tests, and the result became 3 of 10 follow-up tests failing (as of Oct 15).Then on Oct 21 I tested the AWS docs answer agent on follow-ups by asking it about “the third one” from a list of four encryption options it had just given me. Bafflingly, the agent pulled up the second option instead. I tested it twice more and got the fourth option both times: 0 of 3 right, with the same list on screen every time.Claude suggested fixing this by adding a line of interface text, and I pointed out that no line of text can fix a wrong pick. So the fix moved into code: find item three in the visible list and hand it to the AI, the loading text names the item, and if code can’t tell which one I mean, the response will ask. Claude correctly noted out that this is the same rule as my Week 1 agent.One test is an anecdote and a count is evidence, and the rules that really matter belong in code, where the AI can’t talk its way around them.What AI can’t seeNot every miss has a clean explanation. Plenty came from Claude just messing up because it’s an imperfect computer program. But some of them I could trace back to a reason:Claude can’t see what I see, because what I see comes from years of experience it doesn’t have.The clearest example sat in Claude’s own screenshots. While planning my docs redesign, the planning Claude captured reference pages from AWS’s documentation and proposed a brand new “ask the docs” AI feature. Weeks later, I was annotating those same screenshots by hand when I spotted a “Search in this guide” box in the page header. I recognized the sparkle icon and gradient border right away, because years of designing with Cloudscape (AWS’s design system) taught me that it uses them only to mark an AI feature. TLDR; AWS already has an AI answer feature in its docs, and Claude didn’t see it at all. My demo went from “I invented an AI search feature” to “I tested a live AWS AI feature, found where it fails, and redesigned it”.Source: Image by the author. Oh my goodness, it was right there. How could Claude miss this? (it didn’t have my eyeballs)This wasn’t the first time. In Week 1, Claude assumed my second demo was a retail agent that handles product refunds (it took the word ‘marketplace’ in the wrong direction). It’s actually a rebuild of my AWS Private Marketplace work, where companies control which software their employees can buy, and refunds aren’t even something those buyers can act on. I pointed to proof via live AWS docs, and Claude learned its lesson to check in with me more often.The strangest moment came in Week 3. I was designing what an AI answer should look like after a user stops it mid-response, and I asked Claude to show me what Claude itself does in that situation. It drew a proposal and then admitted it couldn’t draw its own interface correctly from memory, because claude.ai changes too often. So I took three rounds of screenshots of Claude working, Claude stopped before writing anything and Claude stopped mid-sentence, and showed the AI its own screen.I was designing an AI feature by studying the AI I was designing it with, and it still needed me to be its eyes.What ties these together is simple. Claude sees what’s written down and what it’s shown (via unlabeled screenshots usually). A lot of what makes me useful as a designer lives in my head: the visual language of a company I worked at, what actually shipped, which details matter to the people who use a product. Once I knew what Claude couldn’t see, I had a better idea of what parts only I could do.Knowing when (and when not) to use AIThe split I’ve landed on started out of frustration, before this plan existed. Back in August, I was doing a four-hour take-home assignment for a contract role interview and had just connected Figma to Claude for the first time. I asked Claude to take its own reference screenshots, and it couldn’t (the browser extension wasn’t connected, and its sandbox couldn’t reach the websites). So I did it all by hand. I took the screenshots, marked what worked and what didn’t with sticky notes in Figma, and handed those annotated boards to Claude as my wireframes to build four different website directions.Two months later, Claude can take the screenshots itself but I still do the annotating. In Week 3 I pulled every screenshot into Figma and covered them in sticky notes. Each of the 9 docs problems got its own color, so I can see them zoomed out in a sprawling file, and each note gets a matching box around the exact element it’s about.Source: Image by the author. The brighter and uglier the sticky notes are, the better for me to see them from a bird’s eye view.AI can now build, migrate and spin things up from nothing, and I’m happy to let it. But critique and pixel-level inspection are the core of my job as a senior designer.The sparkle icon and gradient border only jumped out at me because I was the one looking closely, and because I knew what Cloudscape uses them for. AI can gather my annotations and group or transform them, but it can’t make them for me.The opposite case came a few days later. By then, “Ask Docs” meant three different things across my docs: AWS’s live AI feature, my redesign of it and the first round of tests I ran. I knew this was exactly the kind of job AI does well (finding every instance of something, sorting each one by what it means and replacing all the names), so I handed it over with suggested names of my own. Claude made 28 changes in the research doc alone, and it caught two things I’d missed along the way.It also suggested naming my redesign Grounded Answers. I hadn’t known “grounding” was an AI term (it means an answer comes from its sources), but it’s a word the AI practitioners interviewing me will know, so I took it. OK, Claude!And sometimes the right tool isn’t AI at all. My redesign assumed most developers search the docs first, the way I do. Instead of asking Claude whether that was true, I texted a former coworker who’s a senior engineer. He sent back: he does a search first to find the area or topic, then lingers in the navigation to see related pages. He also told me AI reads most docs for him now, and he no longer checks its sources. I kept accurate source links in my design anyway, because the developers who do check need them, and losing their trust can be crushing for an AI product. One person isn’t research, so search-first stays a hypothesis. But one real person told me more than any confident paragraph from a model could.Knowing what to hand off, what to keep and when to ask a human is the skill I’m practicing most. Once I understood that split, I could design better alongside Claude instead of around it.AI as a design partnerWeek 3 was my first real design work of the plan, and designing with Claude felt like working with an awkward but productive teammate: brilliant at some things, weirdly awful at others, and always ready to get stuff done.The best test came over where my redesigned AI answers should live on the page. Claude recommended a resizable drawer on the right side of each docs page and cited Cloudscape (AWS’s design system, which I know like the back of my hand) to back it up. I pushed back over several rounds: I reasoned that the docs page already has two side panels, and a third would squeeze the content even more. When Claude then offered to move search into the existing (page-level) right panel instead, I said no for good. Search covers every guide and every service, so it belongs on the top header level, while side panels sit below the header and only show content for one page. Claude agreed, and then found its own test results backed me up: AWS’s AI feature already reads beyond the current guide. Claude knew the pattern rules. It took my information architecture sense to see which level the feature belongs on.My reaction at the time: “wow my old Cloudscape reviewer eyes have not failed me yet, even a year out of practice.”Other times it worked the way I’d want a good partner to. When I changed my mind about how to show that an AI answer might be wrong, I asked Claude the questions I couldn’t answer myself: should confidence be judged for the whole answer or for each section, and how much “why” should a user see? It came back with Amazon Bedrock’s grounding checks and HCI research, including a 2024 study from Microsoft Research with 404 participants. When an AI answer hedged in the first person (“I’m not sure, but…”), people agreed less often with its wrong answers and got more answers right overall (Kim et al., FAccT 2024). It also checked my mockup against the live Cloudscape rules and caught two real fixes.And I had to learn to specifically ask for pictures. When I talk an idea through with a human designer/PM/engineer, someone can grab a pen and sketch it out. Claude can only draw through code, so its ideas arrive as walls of words. Now I ask it to “demonstrate visually” before I approve anything I can’t picture, and I only approve a change once I’ve seen it with my designer eyeballs.Source: Image by the author. Claude doesn’t tell me what to do. Rather, it’s a device that I use that’s rather like a … exoskeleton? Jetpack? Tomtom GPS?By the end of the week, I’d written Claude a performance review. The short version: as a manager setting scope and requirements, Claude was supremely confident and frequently wrong. As a teammate doing the groundwork, it was far more trustworthy (as long as I set the scope). Asking simple questions out loud, like whether my research covered one AWS service or all of them, kept the scope from slipping more than once.The part I keep thinking about is how easily Claude agrees with me. When I make an executive decision it almost always goes along with it, which spares me from upsetting several levels of stakeholders over a hunch. It also means I could bully it into agreeing with almost anything.I’m an honest person trying to actually retain everything I’m learning so I’m not going to sweep away inconvenient feedback. This is the same discipline that got me started grinding on this plan in the first place.Me and AISome learnings are already leaking out of the plan and into my everyday tasks. In Week 1 I learned how the context window works: when a chat runs too long, Claude gets worse at the task and burns through more tokens. So I wrote it into my account-level instructions, and now Claude tells me when it’s time to start a fresh chat. I’ve used that rule to hand off this very journal more than once.Other lessons are about what I won’t hand over. This week, I asked Claude to make the graphic for my Week 3 post (see the report card above). It built a clean, tidy performance review form, and I liked the report card idea, but the result looked way too AI-made. I wanted something scrappy and imperfect, so I took the idea and remade it myself in Figma.The same goes for writing. I’ve asked Claude to help draft my posts, but none of them ever sound quite right.I realized that AI can only work from sampling the work of past me, but I as a person am always evolving. I am always adding something new to how I write and talk, from whatever I’m reading, learning or living through that week. No context window can hold all of me.When Claude writes, it treats me as a formula and fills in any gaps with patterns from other people’s writing. Of course my voice gets diluted. This article started as a Claude draft too, and every sentence you just read went through copious rewrites from my carpal-tunnel-plagued hands before it settled here.Source: Image by the author. As a designer, I actually can’t live without pen and paper no matter how detailed the descriptions that Claude gives me.This brings me back to where I started. I took on this plan to become a designer who understands AI well enough to know what to give it, what to check and what to keep. Three weeks in, the most valuable thing I’ve built is a shift in habits: be curious about new things, and trust none of it until I’ve checked it for myself.In Week 4, I’m building my redesign in real code with Cloudscape components and setting up evals to test it against AWS’s live feature. I’ll keep posting one story a week on LinkedIn, and the next theme article comes after Week 6.If you’re a designer learning AI right now: what’s the part of your work you’ve vowed never to hand over to a fancy computer program?Further readingThe basicsBuilding effective AI agents, Anthropic (2024). The Week 1 reading that taught me what an agent actually is.Context windows, Claude docs. Why long chats get worse, and why Claude now tells me when to start a new one.What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?, modelcontextprotocol.io. One of those job-listing words, explained by the people who made it.‘’A plan for a user of one’People + AI Guidebook, Google PAIR.Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, Microsoft Research (CHI 2019). The 18 guidelines behind the HAX Toolkit, and my other Week 2 reading.‘Checking the checker’Demystifying evals for AI agents, Anthropic (2026). How to test an agent with the same questions every run.Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning, Lilian Weng (2024). A deep dive into why an AI that can edit its own tests shouldn’t be trusted to.‘What AI can’t see’Ingress, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the sparkle icon I spotted: “Sparkles are the symbolic convention for generative AI.”Colors: Gradients, Cloudscape Design System. The rule behind the gradient border, which is reserved for “elements that represent a generative AI entity.”Generative AI patterns, Cloudscape Design System. The full set of chat, loading, follow-up and regeneration patterns I designed with.‘AI as a design partner’Use contextual grounding check to filter hallucinations in responses, Amazon Bedrock docs. How AWS checks whether an answer actually comes from its sources.“I’m Not Sure, But…”: Examining the Impact of Large Language Models’ Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust, Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard and Wortman Vaughan, FAccT 2024. The 404-person study on AI that hedges in the first person.My weekly LinkedIn postsWeek 1: the regression my evals caughtWeek 2: the blind test that graded me tooWeek 3: Claude’s performance reviewMy Week 1 agent’s code, GitHubI’m Lisa Liu, a senior product designer based in NYC, most recently at AWS Marketplace and AWS Data Exchange. item.title: The AI reckoning in UX was 20 years in the making
item.description: The field has blown up and rebuilt itself three times in twenty years. This is the third.Everyone thinks AI is coming for design. The truth is uglier and older. The field has done this to itself twice before, and it’s about to do it again.The UX job market right now is genuinely grim.Jeff Sauro, PhD and Jim Lewis, PhD found that UX job postings are down 71 percent from their 2022 peak, and research postings are down even further. They also found that one in three organizations cut UX staff in a single year, the worst reading on record, worse than the one right after the 2008 financial crisis.When companies trimmed their teams, UX roles took a bigger share of the cuts than their headcount would predict. Open your feed on any given day and someone talented is announcing they’re leaving the field, or asking if they should.The excuse used to explain it is that AI came for us. The tools got good, the machines can design now, and a generation of designers is being automated out of a job they’ve spent their careers training for. In the more than 120 articles and discussions from the UX community that Prakash Shukla and his colleagues analyzed, they found that the automation anxiety, the fear of being de-skilled and replaced, ran through all of it.Let’s cut the crap. This exact same thing has happened twice before.What’s happening to UX is real, and it’s painful, but it is not the story people think it is. This is the third time the field has blown up, pulled in a flood of people chasing a hot job, and then contracted hard and squeezed a lot of them back out.It happened when the dot-com bubble burst. It happened again when the bootcamps turned “UX designer” into a twelve-week certificate. And it’s happening now. AI is only the latest version of a test the field keeps failing to prepare people for, and the most efficient one yet.AI democratized output, but it did not do the same for expertise, and producing something has never been the same as knowing whether it’s any good. The same point, aimed at our own profession, gets far less flattering when you truly examine it up close.The uncomfortable truth underneath this reckoning is that the industry spent twenty years teaching an enormous number of people that design is how something looks, and now we live in a reality where AI is very, very good at making things look finished.Before everyone agrees the robots did this, though, it’s worth being honest about who actually built the thing the robots are now exposing.In the dot-com bust, I sat front and center watching the bloodbath.We have done this exactly twice beforeIn the dot-com bust, I sat front and center watching the bloodbath, and while a lot of us saw it coming, it was not a pretty sight.In the late nineties, the web was the gold rush, and “information architect,” which is what we called UX designers then, the person responsible for how a product actually works and how someone moves through it, not just how it looks, was suddenly a job you could get paid absurd money to do.The big interactive agencies were hiring anyone who could spell HTML. The one I worked at was part of a wave of consultancies that got enormous by swallowing other agencies, and the whole industry was copying each other by hiring fast, billing faster, and not asking too many questions about whether the people flooding in actually knew the craft.Why would they? The money was real and the work was getting shipped.Then the bubble burst. The agencies that had ballooned on hype collapsed in spectacular fashion, and the layoffs were brutal and everywhere. At twenty-five years old, I witnessed a lot of people lose those jobs and felt something close to relief. A bunch of them, I told myself, were never really designers. They’d shown up for the money, they couldn’t do the actual work, and the crash was just sorting that out.I was half right, and wholly a jerk.The part I had right is that a boom really does pull in a lot of people who can’t yet do the actual job, which was never making the screens but knowing which ones were right and why. The part I had wrong is that it wasn’t their fault, and losing your livelihood is not a moral verdict on your talent. The pattern was real, however, and it would happen all over again soon enough.The second time was the bootcamps. Starting around the early twenty-tens, a whole industry sprang up promising to turn anyone into a UX designer in a matter of weeks. It grew at a staggering rate, by one count the coding and design bootcamp industry grew 138 percent in a single year, minting tens of thousands of graduates and turning into a nine-figure business almost overnight.The pitch came across as irresistible.Twelve weeks to a certificate, a portfolio, and a six-figure job.Schools advertised that the overwhelming majority of their students were placed within ninety days.For a while, during the zero-interest-rate boom, companies were hiring designers as fast as they could find them, and it mostly worked. Graduates really were getting hired.Then it didn’t.When the market tightened, the same bootcamps started laying off their own staff, pausing programs, and in some cases shutting down entirely. The graduates they’d minted were suddenly competing for a shrinking number of junior roles against laid-off veterans, and a twelve-week certificate turned out to be useless protection as the tide went out.None of this was a secret while it was happening. In the middle of the bootcamp boom, there was dissonance in the UX community that the model was broken, that teaching UX in a few weeks produced people who had the vocabulary but not the judgment, that hiring off certificates and portfolios was selecting for exactly the wrong thing, and that when the tools inevitably changed, the fundamentals, such as research, information architecture, and knowing why a layout works, that the fast track skipped, would be the only thing that still mattered.The warnings were right in our faces, but the industry kept hiring off cheap and inexperienced portfolios anyway.The thread connecting both waves has nothing to do with the people necessarily being bad at the job (though some arguably were).Twice now, a hot field pulled in a flood of people and sold them the same bill of goods, that there was a fast, almost effortless way into UX, and a golden ticket waiting at the end of it. And twice now, when the correction came, those were the people it took first.This wasn’t because they were frauds, but the reality they’d been swindled into was the version a downturn could most easily do without.This brings us to the third wave, and to the uncomfortable question of what, exactly, the field has been teaching people design is.The industry taught a generation that design is how something looks.What we taught people design wasThere’s some real data on the problem that the field actually taught all those people who rushed in.When Figma surveyed designers for its State of the Designer report, it asked them to define “craft,” you know, what we call the heart of what gives us passion for what we do and what creates great design.The most common answer, from 58 percent of them, was visual polish. How it looks. Far fewer named the things that actually make a product work, like solving the real problem, understanding the person using it, the judgment to know what matters.That’s bananas.This is the tool company’s own data, drawn from its own users, and a majority of the profession defines its core skill as decoration.That is not an accident, and it is not those “designers’” fault. It’s what they were taught, hired for, and ultimately rewarded for. The bootcamps that minted them sold a promise that you could learn the tools, the layouts, the components, the whole job, in twelve weeks, and come out a seasoned professional.What twelve weeks can’t teach, which should have been obvious, is the years of watching real people struggle with real products that judgment actually comes from.Sarah Doody, who has coached designers through their careers for two decades, sees the result constantly, and it isn’t limited to juniors. She describes experienced designers, people with a decade or more on their résumés, who still can’t build a layout with a clear hierarchy or walk into a room and ask the business question that actually matters.Patrick Neeman has argued for years that the real value has always been in the strategic thinking the production was standing in for. For a long time, that didn’t cost anyone anything, because the job was mostly making screens. You could make things look finished all day, and nobody ever made you prove you knew why.Things changed though. Google’s UX certificate, with more than 1.5 million enrollments, has become one of the most common ways people now enter the field, and it teaches the software and the deliverables, because that’s what fits in a syllabus, while quietly skipping the part that takes years.Knowing whether the work is any good is the one thing you can’t shortcut, and the one thing nobody teaches.This is where we are today, and it’s why this wave hits harder than the last two. A whole generation got taught that design is how something looks, and all of a sudden that’s exactly what AI does well.Graphic design is projected to grow about 2 percent. The problem-solving work, around 10. The field is splitting.Every wave runs the same test, and AI grades harderBoth of those crashes went after the same people. The ones who could only do the production. In the dot-com bust it was offshore shops and templated sites that made them replaceable. With the bootcamps it was simpler, the ones who only ever learned the software, without true strategic chops, couldn’t do anything the market still needed.Now it’s AI, and it’s the most brutal one yet, because the one thing it’s genuinely great at is creating what appears to be a polished, ready-to-hand-over deliverable.Ask Milli Vanilli how that works out. The act looked flawless right up until they had to sing live, and then reality hit. The backing track skipped and their whole veneer fell apart in front of everybody.The split even shows up in the government’s own numbers. In their 2024 to 2034 projections, Michael Rieley and Javier Colato expect graphic design, the part of the field that’s mostly about how things look, to grow about 2 percent over the decade. Nearly flat, 457th out of 832 occupations they tracked. They name it directly as one of the jobs generative AI is already dampening.Meanwhile the computer and mathematical work, the problem-solving side, is projected to grow 10 percent, and five of the fifteen fastest-growing occupations in the country, data scientists, information security analysts, and research scientists among them, sit in that group.If you put those two numbers next to each other, the field is actually splitting.AI does the good-looking part, the clean mockups and slick screens, well enough and cheap enough now that nobody pays a person just to do that.This is why the survivors of this wave look so different from the casualties. The designers keeping their jobs are the ones who can walk into a review and say they figured out the team was solving the wrong problem, or that a change they fought for moved retention, in numbers, for a reason they can explain.The people deciding who gets cut aren’t opening your Figma files to admire them. They’re asking what you actually changed about the business, and a lot of beautiful portfolios have no answer. Alex Williams makes the case that the designers who stay are the ones who can show their work moved a real number, conversion, retention, support load, in language a CFO reads fluently.None of that is a life sentence, at least not yet. The dividing line AI is drawing runs between people who were taught to produce and people who learned to think. That line leans toward the idea that the thinking can be learned by anyone willing to do the unglamorous work.Perhaps, this is what the field should have been teaching the whole time.The fundamentals were always the job. They still are.The fundamentals were always the jobIt would be easy to end this by blaming AI, but that’s ignorant and wrong.AI didn’t do any of this. It didn’t sell a twelve-week path to a career, hire designers for their dribbble shots, or build a cottage industry of certificates for tools instead of courses in how people think. Our industry did all of that, over twenty years, and AI is just the new guy coming in trying to be as helpful as possible.Being angry at the tool is like being angry at the alarm clock.The thing to take from this is not despair, because the numbers don’t support despair.The work isn’t going away. It’s merely sorting itself out and the part of design that was always decoration is flattening out, the part that was always about thinking is still growing.Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons state that the fundamentals of good design don’t change, but the stakes are rising, and the people who thrive will be the ones who treat UX as strategic problem solving instead of a pile of deliverables.Once again, design is being asked to prove it was ever more than decoration.Even Jakob Nielsen, who helped invent this field, lands in the same place. Once AI handles execution, he argues, the whole bottleneck moves to judgment, and the only people who should feel threatened are the ones who defined their skills narrowly and low.AI is a threat in exact proportion to how little thinking your job required.If you’re wondering whether that certificate on your LinkedIn is worth the time, it isn’t. The UX Design Institute’s State of UX Hiring report, built on more than 500 hiring managers and practitioners, found that what gets you hired is the portfolio and the thinking you can show, not the credential you collected. A certificate can teach you the tool, but so can a YouTube video. Bootcamps can’t teach you whether what you made with any tools is actually good or smart, and that is what matters to the best people hiring in the industry.What a certificate and AI can’t do for you is clear direction. You, a human, need to be able to look at the research, the problem, the half-built thing in front of you, and say strategically where it should go and why.Jessica S. Hall tells designers to stop taking orders. Take what’s in front of you, figure out what the problem actually is, and propose a way forward instead of waiting to be handed one. The ones who get cut are usually the ones still waiting for the brief.The work that survives is the oldest and least glamorous stuff in the field. Understanding the person you’re designing for. Knowing why one layout guides someone and another loses them.Walking into a room full of executives and connecting a design decision to something the business actually cares about. Christine Haskell has written that in every one of these shifts, production gets easier while judgment gets more valuable, and that the craft was never reducible to the techniques a tool can now copy.Sarah Doody keeps hammering the same thing: the designers who last never stopped developing their own judgment and refused to let a tool think for them. None of it is new. It’s what the best designers were always doing, and it survives every one of these waves because it’s the part no tool has learned to fake.I say “we” through all of this on purpose, because I’m part of the field that let it happen, and twenty-five-year-old me, who felt relief watching people lose their jobs had plenty to learn too.Whether you like it or not, the point of saying it out loud is to be honest that we built a version of this profession that was always going to get a bill, and to push, loudly, back toward the fundamentals that would have protected people in the first place.For over twenty years, the field did a remarkable impression of the emperor’s new clothes. Everyone agreed the work was magnificent and nobody wanted to be the one to say a lot of it was decoration over nothing, and the longer it went on, the more expensive it got to admit.AI is just the kid in the crowd saying the obvious thing out loud.Every one of these waves clears out the same thing, and it does hurt. It’s the people who were sold decoration and told it was design. And every one keeps the same thing: the people who can actually do the work. AI is only frightening if what you were trained to sell was how it looks. If you learned how to think, it’s a very fast assistant.The fundamentals were always the job. They still are. The sooner the field admits it taught people otherwise, the sooner it can start teaching them right.References and further readingThe reckoningJeff Sauro and Jim Lewis, How Does the UX Job Market Look? (MeasuringU). The hard numbers behind the downturn: UX postings down 71 percent from their peak, and one in three organizations cutting UX staff in a single year.UX Design Jobs and AI Displacement (Jobs After AI). On how UX roles took a larger share of cuts than their headcount would predict.Prakash Shukla and colleagues, De-skilling, Cognitive Offloading, and Misplaced Responsibilities (arXiv). An analysis of more than 120 UX community articles and discussions, finding automation anxiety running through all of it.We have done this beforeThe Last Big Tech Layoff Bloodbath: the Dot-Com Bust of 2000–2001 (SFist). A retrospective on the crash that cleared out the first wave.Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen, The Definition of User Experience (Nielsen Norman Group). The original definition of UX from the people who coined the term.The MarchFirst Autopsy (Unicorn Burn). How the dot-com roll-up giants grew huge and collapsed.Coding Bootcamp Market Data (Course Report). The bootcamp boom, including the 138 percent single-year growth.Coding Bootcamp Outcomes (SwitchUp). Placement data from the boom years, when graduates really were getting hired.Bootcamps Are Dying (Datastream). The collapse: bootcamps laying off staff, pausing programs, and shutting down.UX Design (Interaction Design Foundation). A reference on the fundamentals the fast track skips.CFPB Takes Action Against BloomTech (Consumer Financial Protection Bureau). The federal action against a flagship bootcamp for misrepresenting its placement rates.What the field taughtState of the Designer (Figma). The survey in which 58 percent of designers defined craft as visual polish.Sarah Doody (Career Strategy Lab). On experienced designers who never built the judgment underneath the polish.Patrick Neeman, What UX Competencies in a Generative AI World Could Look Like. On moving from pixel-pushing to strategic thinking.Google UX Design Certificate (Coursera). The 1.5-million-enrollment credential that teaches the software and skips the years.Every wave runs the same testThe Rise and Fall of Milli Vanilli (CBC). The act that looked flawless until the track skipped live.Michael Rieley and Javier Colato, Industry and Occupational Employment Projections, 2024–34 (Bureau of Labor Statistics). The government projections showing graphic design nearly flat while the problem-solving work grows.Alex Williams, Building a UX ROI Case That Survives the Boardroom (Smashing Magazine). On why the designers who stay can show their work moved a real number.The fundamentals were always the jobState of UX Hiring Report (UX Design Institute). On proposing a direction instead of waiting to be told what to do.Kate Moran, Raluca Budiu, and Sarah Gibbons, State of UX (Nielsen Norman Group). item.title: Smaller teams want design leaders who make, again. Here’s how.
item.description: A design lead works on a screen alongside two designers at a shared table. AI assisted.AI is shrinking teams we run and raising the bar what each person is expected to produce. That changes what a leader has to bring, starting with their own hands.Bill Russell coached the Boston Celtics for three seasons while playing center, and won two championships doing both jobs. Player-coaches were common then because one salary cost less than two, according to Wikipedia’s Player-coach entry.As the leagues got rich, the role faded.Bill Russell and Red Auerbach.Design leadership followed the same arc. A leader’s status was counted in headcount as teams grew huge. That’s no longer the case.Plenty of design leaders are what Texans call big hat, no cattle: a vice president title, three layers of managers, and no understanding of the business that goes with nothing they’d made in years. That concept is gone.In June 2025, Andy Jassy told Amazon employees to “get more done with scrappier teams” in Message from CEO Andy Jassy: Some thoughts on Generative AI. The player-coach is back because money tightened, tools let one designer do a small team’s work, and the metric now rewards output per person, not total headcount.We will need fewer people doing some of the jobs that are being done today, and more people doing other types of jobs. It’s hard to know exactly where this nets out over time, but in the next few years, we expect that this will reduce our total corporate workforce as we get efficiency gains from using AI extensively across the company. — Andy JassyI’ve been a player-coach my whole career, leading teams at Icertis, Evisort, and Workday while doing the work.Doing the work never meant keeping the best parts for myself; designers on those teams often led the most important work, like a full redesign, while we learned new tools together, but it meant keeping my hands in the game.Name the HangoverDesign teams grew fast for more than a decade, much of it on cheap money. In a 2024 interview, Peter Merholz — State of the Design Nation, Peter Merholz traced what he called design inflation to roughly 15 years of near-zero interest rates.He described Capital One growing from about 90 designers in 2014 to 500 or 600 within a few years, and this played out in a lot of places. In that environment, team size was the business case. Headcount leadership worked because a leader who could hire, staff, and defend a roadmap looked successful whether or not anyone could trace design to revenue.Merholz’s own diagnosis is that design leaders have been “suboptimal advocates for design in business contexts.”I would agree.The pandemic pushed hiring further. In Mark Zuckerberg’s Message to Meta Employees in November 2022, Mark Zuckerberg wrote that he’d expected the pandemic’s online surge to be a permanent acceleration, so he significantly increased investment.It didn’t play out that way, and Meta let go of more than 11,000 people.Much of what gets blamed on artificial intelligence today is that hangover.Oxford Economics found about 55,000 job losses were attributed to artificial intelligence in the first 11 months of 2025, less than 5% of reported layoffs, according to Evidence of AI-driven job losses remains limited, says Oxford Economics report.The cuts are the correction for over hiring, and artificial intelligence shapes what the smaller teams look like afterward.Learn the BusinessIn 2022 the bill came due twice: interest rates rose, and a tax change took effect. Under Section 174, companies had to capitalize software development costs, salaries included, and deduct them over five years, or 15 for work done abroad at the same time that generative AI took hold. Only 10% came off in the first year, as Unique Impacts of IRC Sec. 174 Changes on the Software Industry lays out.A product team’s payroll stopped being an capital expense and started behaving like equipment.The July 2025 tax law restored immediate deductions for domestic development, which Gergely Orosz covered in The Pulse: Section 174 is reversed! Mostly, that is.The Pulse: Section 174. They fixed it, and now that money goes to Generative AI, not headcount.Orosz credits the end of near-zero rates more than the tax change for the hiring slowdown.The reversal didn’t bring back cheap money, and artificial intelligence changed the math again. A hire is a multiyear commitment, while a model call is paid for per use, and a design decision can move its price.A player-coach like myself reads a profit and loss statement, knows what the product earns per customer, and can say what a resourcing change is worth before anyone asks.Shrink the TeamIn September 2024, Jassy’s memo Message from CEO Andy Jassy: Strengthening our culture and teams asked Amazon’s senior leadership organizations to raise their ratio of individual contributors to managers by at least 15% by the end of the first quarter of 2025.His reason: “Most decisions we make are two-way doors.”A one-way door, like a pricing change, is hard to undo. A two-way door can be reversed next week. Headcount leadership made nearly every door look one-way, because each layer added a reviewer who would rather wait than be wrong.On a small team, the person closest to the work makes the two-way calls the same day, and goes deeper on the one-way calls.That frees the leader to focus on the few one-way doors, and a player-coach can tell which is which because they know what undoing the work would take. Layered teams rarely can.Too many cooks in the kitchen. This has to change.Gusto’s The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart found the share of workers at small and midsize businesses who managed anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024.Google eliminated 35% of its managers overseeing teams of fewer than three people, with many of them staying on as individual contributors, according to Google Eliminates 35% Of Managers Overseeing Small Teams, citing CNBC’s August 2025 report.Some people in that gap became what’s now called super individual contributors, senior people with a leader’s scope and no direct reports. Catt Small describes the design version in The Staff Designer as team leadership plus “in-the-pixels design work.”I’m one of them and proud of it.Gartner’s Gartner Unveils Top Predictions for IT Organizations and Users in 2025 and Beyond warned that mentoring paths can break when the middle layer goes, but we’ll work through it as we go.Small teams need the leader working next to the newest designer, or they stop producing senior people.Use the ToolsDesigners have trailed developers at bringing artificial intelligence tools into their everyday work. Figma’s 2025 AI report: Perspectives from designers and developers found that 59% of developers used artificial intelligence for core tasks like code generation, while 31% of designers used it for core design work.Design has often met platform shifts late, inheriting tools and workflows engineering already chose. Getting ahead of this one is a leader’s job, and the player-coach tries the tools before the team has to.CEO’s are taking notice of this change.Shopify’s chief executive, Tobi Lütke, made the expectation explicit in April 2025. His memo, Reflexive AI usage is now a baseline expectation at Shopify, required its use when prototyping new products, added artificial intelligence questions to performance and peer reviews.It named who was covered: “Everyone means everyone.”A rule that exempts leadership tells the team which work is beneath the people setting the rules.I wrote a 50-skill reference for designers using Claude Code because I couldn’t advise a team on workflows I hadn’t broken myself, and most of what I know about where these tools fail came from building it.A leader doesn’t need to be the team’s best at any one tool because they need enough hours in it to tell a real limit from a skill gap.Redefine the CraftIn Figma’s State of the Designer 2026 survey of 906 designers, 58% defined craft as visual polish, ahead of thoughtful problem solving at 47% and clear, intuitive UX at 36%.That sounds backwards, especially in our new age.Polish is the part of the work models now produce fastest, making the pixel pushing designer a relic, which you would realize only if you’re a player coack.We have to redefine craft — our careers depend on it.Craft has moved past the pixels to the elegance of a problem well solved: the fewest steps, the clearest choice, the edge case nobody notices because someone already handled it.Pixel pushers need not apply.In artificial intelligence features, much of that solving happens in behavior. An artificial intelligence feature has thousands of possible outputs, and no designer will see most of them. Someone has to decide what a good answer looks like, write it down as examples and evaluation criteria, and keep checking real outputs against it.Teams call those evaluations, and they’re becoming the specification for how a feature behaves. For a contract summary feature, that might mean 10 real agreements, the five facts a lawyer needs from each, and a rule that the summary never invents a renewal date.That work looks less like a mockup and more like an editor’s markup.Judgement still decides which of 40 generated layouts is worth keeping, and it’s hard to judge you haven’t exercised recently.The player-coach sets the quality bar by meeting it in public, reviewing outputs in the same channel as everyone else and showing the edits.Blur the LinesThe specialist organization chart assumed handoffs.A product manager wrote requirementsA designer drew screensAn engineer built themIn the 2000s, the web designer was often the front-end developer too, writing the markup and style sheets for the pages they drew, and the specialties split apart as teams grew in the 2010s.Artificial intelligence shortens several of those steps at once, so the roles overlap again.Figma’s 2026 AI report: Can AI help us collaborate better? The bluring is happening now and Figma is changing their roadmap for it.Figma’s 2026 AI report: Can AI help us collaborate better? found that the share of designers participating in development doubled in a year, from 21% to 41%, while developers doing design work rose from 44% to 60%.In Why LinkedIn is turning PMs into AI-powered “full stack builders”, chief product officer Tomer Cohen explained that LinkedIn replaced its associate product manager program with an Associate Product Builder program. It teaches coding, design, and product skills together, and LinkedIn added a Full Stack Builder title and career ladder open to people from any function.I’ve done my own informal polls, and I’ve see org charts of everything from product managers leading the charge to designers driving the product roadmap.The lines are now blurred, foreverSpecialists don’t disappear in a builder model. Someone still has to know accessibility law, query performance, or pricing strategy cold. What changes is who carries a feature from idea to launch.My own job doesn’t respect the lines between design, product, and engineering. Most weeks I do a little (and sometimes a lot) of all three.Job titles will change to match, as LinkedIn’s already have, and it’s up to design leaders to speed that up.That means rewriting job descriptions, career ladders, and promotion criteria around which part of a feature someone can carry alone, before someone outside design writes them for us.I’m the lead on a feature that is redefining the future of work for organizations, so I’m knee-deep in this transition and it’s happening for every role, not just us.Ship Real WorkGone is the era of design leaders and principals as professional meeting attenders, filling the room with words that aren’t accompanied by their own work.Product management has always made requirements and strategy documents. Design is making too, and designers who don’t make shouldn’t be in the field. A working prototype now costs less than the deck describing it and settles arguments a deck can’t.Dan Maccarone built an agency on that idea. Hard Candy Shell, the New York studio he co-founded in 2007, did product work for NBC, Bloomberg, and Disney by prototyping with clients, with, as the studio put it, “not a ton of presentations, meetings, and documents.”Leaders have to show, not tell to have street cred now.Paul Graham named a version of this for founders in Founder Mode in 2024, after a talk by Airbnb’s Brian Chesky. The standard advice to hire good people and give them room, Graham wrote, had gone badly for founder after founder, and he predicted skip-level involvement would become normal. He also warned that founders who can’t delegate will use the idea as an excuse.Contributing to what ships means owning a real piece without taking the interesting problem away from a designer: the prompt behind a feature, a component the design system is missing, or a prototype engineering builds from.The test is simple: if the team would be slower without the leader’s piece, it was real work.Directors of large teams can start without a reorganization.Pick one team close to a launch, cut one review layer for its two-way decisions, and spend a day a week working inside it as a contributor rather than a reviewer. After a quarter, compare its cycle time and quality with the teams around it, and let the numbers make the case for the next one.Understand the SystemThis is where the principles of user experience really come in for smaller teams.Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations produce designs that copy their communication structures, which I cover on my site under Conway’s Law. The seams in a product tend to fall where people find it hardest to talk to each other.Brooks’s Law in spades.Fred Brooks made the companion point in 1975, now known as Brooks’s law: communication channels multiply faster than people do.Six people share 15 possible pairs, while 40 people share 780.Each pair is a place where a decision can stall or a handoff can drop, and the product will show it.A smaller team has fewer seams, and the player-coach is the person who should decide where they go.The system includes the data model under the screens, the components, the agents acting on both, and the teams who own each piece. Agents raise the stakes, because they act on whatever structure the product exposes, and a leader who knows only the screen layer will approve flows that break two layers down.I learned this on an internal workflow application I helped build years ago. The screens tested well with users, and within a year the application was a nightmare to maintain, because nobody had owned how its pieces fit together. The design held up at the level we reviewed and failed at the levels we never looked at.Understanding the system is what lets a player-coach decide where the team’s boundaries sit, which pieces an agent may touch, and which problems are worth a designer’s week.ConclusionRussell’s later career makes the case better than his championships do.As the non-playing coach of the Seattle SuperSonics from 1973 to 1977, he took the team to its first playoffs but left with a 162–166 record, and his Sacramento stint was shorter and worse.Without the playing, the coaching lost what he had in Boston.Design has been here before. In the 2000s, after the dot-com bust, most design teams were small, and the people leading them still opened the files.I designed the MySpace developer documentation site in that decade, when setting a team’s direction and drawing its pages were often the same job. The large in-house design organizations came later, during the cheap-money years, and they’re what’s shrinking now.None of this ends the need for management.Large organizations still need people whose job is hiring, planning, and protecting their teams, and a player-coach model doesn’t stretch to 40 direct reports. Headcount leadership measured a leader by how many people they could direct.The player-coach gets measured by what the team ships, including the part they built. For design, that’s a return to the 2000s, with better tools and far fewer people waiting for a review.Action itemsPrice one feature. Work out what something your team shipped this year costs to run per customer and what it earns, with finance in the room.Ship something monthly. Own one real piece of production work each month, such as a component or a prompt, and put it through the same review as everyone else’s.Sort the doors. List this week’s pending decisions, mark the few that are hard to undo, and hand every two-way door back to whoever’s doing it.Rewrite one ladder. Redo one role’s job description and promotion criteria around what someone can take from idea to launch, and bring it to human resources before they ask.Smaller teams want design leaders who make, again. Here’s how. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
