item.title: Going nowhere fast
item.description: When speed disguises itself as progress.One driver worked hard to get to a stoplight. (Rounded Bevel Icons by Tristan)I distinctly remember my father driving the speed limit down a two-way street in the Bronx when a car swung out from behind us and cut into our lane with a few feet to spare. It wasn’t the first time, and whenever it happened, I’d anticipate his favorite phrase, delivered with zero road rage, “Going nowhere fast.”Twenty seconds later, we rolled up to a red light, with the car that cut us off sitting right next to us. One question that stayed with me as a curious 12-year-old: “Did they notice?” Did the driver notice that, after all that effort to get ahead, their reward was a red light? Did speed feel like progress to them?Speed that feels like progressDrivers act on the information they have and make quick decisions. Empty lane. I can go around and make the next light. The reality is that many traffic lights run on a timed sequence. Beating one light will often get you to the next red light sooner. The driver who cut us off will almost always remember the pass, not the light. The cost will not appear where the shortcut was taken, but will show up later. By then it’ll be easy to miss what caused it.Today, product teams are in that lane. For decades we’ve leaned on a tidy rule, GIGO (garbage in, garbage out). It assumed the garbage was obvious. With AI, it isn’t. Garbage goes in and comes out polished, making “beating the system” look like winning. AI can’t weigh what’s true for your users; it predicts what’s likely. Feed it your own data (interview notes, support tickets, instrumentation data), and the polish has truth underneath it. Feed it a guess, and it’ll output a guess with confidence.Atlassian’s State of Product 2026 report found that product managers gain nearly two hours a day with AI, yet most still feel stuck in reactive mode, and 84% have concerns their products won’t succeed. Speed increased. Confidence did not. Faster output isn’t the same as assurance that you’re building the right thing.When AI takes the wheelDrivers who cut through traffic are under pressure, and an opening looks like an opportunity. Starting with AI works the same way. Ask it for user needs, customer experience maps, and personas, and you’ll have results in minutes. Results that can leave you with false confidence that you’ve found the exact problem you’re solving for. Defining a problem solely within an LLM’s capabilities lets AI do the heavy lifting based on averages, preexisting biases, and general patterns of what’s been written about the thing you’re trying to solve. And the output is often opaque, forcing teams to trace back why conclusions emerged or what assumptions shaped them, frequently hitting a dead end.This is top-down thinking, and it doesn’t address your customer’s pain today. Relying on AI before meaningful design discovery can be tremendously costly. It eats up engineering and design time, causes organizational toil for product teams, and creates disruptions that show up much later. In high-stakes areas like hiring, fintech, lending, and healthcare, it can cause great harm.Bottom-up thinking begins with humans. It involves research to define a problem and understand the systems connected to it, with all of their interdependent parts. It’s messy work, like mapping how a need links to complex networks and processes orbiting around it. It lets teams be wrong early, when it’s cheap. It’s a route that unpacks what’s unique and specific to your users. This is where AI becomes useful, by processing your users’ needs once you’ve observed them.The synthetic research trapIn Thinking in Systems, Donella Meadows unpacks a trap called ‘rule beating’, following the letter of a rule to circumvent its purpose.Thinking in Systems by Donella H. MeadowsShe highlights this with a Calvin and Hobbes strip by Bill Watterson:In the comic strip, Calvin tells Hobbes he’ll do ten good deeds daily until Christmas so Santa goes easy on him. When Hobbes points out Susie (his nemesis) is “coming this way,” Calvin decides he’ll start tomorrow and do twenty a day.Calvin isn’t trying to be benevolent. He hopes to catch up on a year of bad behavior to look good for Santa.Synthetic research (AI-generated) participants can work the same way. One of the most widely cited principles in UX and human-centered design is to understand your users before you build. Synthetic personas let teams check the research box without meeting a single user.Research isn’t just about avoiding the average. It’s the only way to get the newest answer.When NN/g re-ran three of its own studies using AI-generated participants, it found the answers were too shallow to be helpful. In one study, the synthetic participants claimed they had completed each course. The research looked complete, but the answers were too good to be true.In a 2026 User Interviews survey of 150 researchers, 81% used AI regularly in their work, but only 8% used it to simulate participants. Their biggest concerns were the quality and accuracy of insights (88%) and stakeholders overly trusting AI-generated findings (79%).The newest answer lives in the field.Your users’ behavior is the newest and truest information that you have. Their workarounds from last month, the rage clicks that began after the last release, net new needs that started to bubble up this quarter after industry shifts. They exist only in the field. Your product’s newest nuances won’t reliably surface in any training data. Research isn’t just about avoiding the average. It’s the only way to get the newest answer.Meadows’ way out isn’t adding more rules. It’s redesigning them so that people’s efforts go toward the goal instead of around it. For product teams, it means measuring whether we understand our users, not whether we produced a persona or archetype. A research finding can trace back to something tangible, an interview or a support ticket.What discovery can revealConsider a product team asked to speed up the permissions workflow in an admin console. To move quickly, they prompt AI to create an admin persona. The persona is convincing; busy, technical, and frustrated by too many clicks.The obvious solution follows: 1. Bulk actions2. Fewer confirmations3. Single click to apply changes across the organizationThen a designer, PM, and developer spend a week with five real admins, and a completely different theme emerges. They want to move faster, but speed isn’t their biggest worry. Mistakes are. One wrong change can lock hundreds of people out of their tools or give the wrong group access to sensitive information.Illustration conveys an ‘Apply to everyone on click’, with other team members locked out.They don’t need fewer steps. What they need is confidence:• A preview of who a change will affect• A record of what changed and when• An easy and clear way to undoWith these in place, bulk actions stop being a risk and become the speedup that the team asked for.The AI persona wasn’t wrong that administrators are busy. It was average. It described what admins in general say, not what these administrators risk. Building on personas alone, the team would have shipped a faster way to make costly mistakes, and found out months later through support escalations and lost trust.Misapplied speed shows up in costly support tickets.Discovery did not slow the team down. It gave AI detail to work with. Once the team had transcripts and a quarter’s worth of support tickets, the LLM ranked failure scenarios, drafted audit-log requirements, and generated concepts for previews and undo flows. With the same LLM, the input was now grounded in what actual customers are experiencing. As a result, they built something the admin (at the center of their product) actually values.…your competitors don’t have exactly what your users told youDiscovery turns “apply to everyone” into a preview of who the changes affect.Discovery and research first, then accelerateSpeed isn’t the problem. Rule beating is. Once humans have begun the work, AI becomes a powerful accelerator. It synthesizes interview notes, spots patterns, generates concept variations, and sharpens questions you can bring to the next round of research. The difference is that it’s working from your users.Discovery gives you two advantages over teams racing toward the next light:You stay out of their pileup: Unvalidated work drains teams with costly rework, organizational toil, and disruption after shipping a feature. Teams doing discovery aren’t in that collision.You expose their blind spot and see what they can’t: Every competitor has access to the same models, and anyone can quickly spin up a product spec and render an outcome in seconds. The real advantage is that your competitors don’t have exactly what your users told you.To this day, my father has never won a race to a red light. He’s also never been in an accident. Decades of driving throughout the metro area, and not a single pileup. He isn’t slow. He just knows how the road works.Real leverage today doesn’t come from flooring it with every new AI capability. It comes from anchoring the tool to what you’ve learned from your users and understanding the road beneath you. That’s how you get where you’re actually trying to go, and take your customers with you.They will notice.Fast. Safe. Confident. What five admins told the product team is needed.Originally published October 19th, 2026Over the past decade, I’ve focused on designing product experiences for developers within multidisciplinary teams. I’ve led design for IaC adoption, incident management, and observability within socio-technical environments.Resources:APA: Meadows, D.H. (2008). Thinking in Systems: A primer. item.title: Building an AI-ready design system library: Code → Figma with MCP.
item.description: In-System DesignA practical guide for designers: why my design system starts in code, and how I build, check and maintain the Figma library.In-System Design: a three-part series.Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)For designers who know Figma well and have never written production code, and for the design system teams around them. Every technical word is explained in the box at the end.For most of my career, the work went one way. I designed in Figma, a developer turned it into code, and when something did not survive the trip, we sorted it out between us.Then I handed that same route to an AI, and what came back was unsettling, mainly because it looked fine. It read my Figma file, translated it faithfully, and filled in everything the file did not say with whatever seemed plausible.The code that comes out is mediocre, and that is the part everyone frets about. Fair enough, since code quality is at least the part you can read, review and complain about in a pull request.What worries me more is what gets invented: the focus order, the error states, what a screen reader announces, what happens when a request fails, or when a list comes back empty. None of that shows up in a screenshot, so nobody catches it in review.So I turned the direction around. My design system now starts in code, and I generate my Figma library from it. Code always wins, and Figma is a mirror, not a second truth.That sounds like a demotion for Figma, and in practice my Figma file got busier. This article is why, how I build the library, and how I keep an existing one honest, including the parts that still need babysitting.Why doesn’t Figma-to-code with AI work well?Because your Figma file was always supposed to be an abstraction. Let me explain: I sat down one afternoon and compared what a React component can express with what a Figma component can express, because that is the kind of thing I do for fun now, apparently. The life and soul of the party, I am. My count came out at roughly 17% coverage. For CSS, it was better, around 45%, and still nowhere near complete.Those are my own numbers from my own comparison, not an official statistic. Check them against your own stack before quoting them in a meeting.Everything Figma cannot say used to be filled in by a developer who could walk over and ask a question.That gap is not a Figma failure, and no, I do not want Figma to close it. If focus order, container behaviour and ARIA labels lived in the file, you would need to be a front-end developer to use your own library.A developer also notices what is missing. An AI does not. It takes the file literally, as a complete instruction, fills the gaps with whatever it has seen most often, and carries on, so the old direction now produces a component that looks finished and is partly invented.Turn the arrow around and the same literal-mindedness becomes a gift. Generating from code, “it reads exactly what is there” is precisely what you want, because what is there is the real thing: real props, real values, real defaults, real states.Flip it: Code as the source of truth, Figma followsCode is the source of truth. Figma mirrors it. Where they differ, Figma is wrong.I know how that lands in a room full of designers. Designers still do not work in code, and I have no plans to write production code myself. Figma does not matter less either. I think best on a canvas; I design there, and I would fight anyone who tried to take it away, so hear me out.Hands-on: from a repo to a Figma library, step by step:This is the workflow I currently use and demo, with the prompts I actually use. You don’t need to be a developer for this. You do need to be comfortable opening a repo and reading what’s in it, and the AI will walk you through the rest. So yes, some new territory, but stay with me! It’s great fun!What you need: 1. A design system in code you can access, with Storybook running on it2. An empty Figma file3. MCP connection. I use and recommend Figma Console MCP by Southleft for this because it reads and writes variables properly, which the basic connection does not.1. Get access to the code as a designerA branch, a sandbox, or a playground repo. Ask development for the smallest safe thing: a copy where nothing you do can reach production.If you want to practise first, download any sample design system as a zip and point your AI at the folder. I hand out a sample file for trainings and sessions, but you can also make your own. Connect that folder or branch with your AI. I will use Claude Code for my example. Your developers will most likely use the terminal or an editor; I use the Claude desktop app and the Claude Code tab.2. Check that Storybook is thereOnce you are connected, ask Claude Code to open Storybook for you.What you get is a local website: it runs on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001. Only you can see it, nothing is published, and it is built from the code sitting in front of you. It shows every component, live and clickable.Storybook does not keep its own copy of your system; it lives inside it. Next to each component sits a small stories file listing its examples, so the page you click through is built from the real code and you can see, understand and compare it as a designer. That is also the key to prototyping with AI and generating sensible output, and I will come back to it in another article.It is so great to finally go through the real stuff visually as a designer; I cannot believe I didn’t use this earlier! You can look at the Storybook of one of my samples here.No Storybook? You can still do everything in this article. What you lose is the view and the component list, which I personally need to understand and compare, and for some parity checks later on.If you are in a playground environment, you can just ask Claude to add it to your own copy and play there. In a real repo, it is a developer’s call, because it brings dependencies somebody has to maintain, so ask rather than install. It also needs to be Storybook 10 or newer, with the components manifest switched on, before an agent can read that list (this is for parity checks and prototyping later).3. Open an empty Figma fileClean, empty, and destined to become the library. Not your existing library, which comes later. Then open the Console MCP inside it.From here, Claude Code is the hub between the two: one arm in the real code, one in the open Figma file. I can ask in plain words for something to be read on one side and built on the other.4. Tokens and styles first, alwaysComponents use tokens, so the tokens and text styles have to exist before the components do.First find out where the tokens live, and yes, you can just ask Claude. In my repo they are JSON: one layer of raw values, one of semantic roles. In yours they might be CSS custom properties, or a Tailwind config, in which case I am sorry. Figma then splits them into two: colours, spacing and radii become variables, typography becomes text styles bound to variables. Console MCP does this well; you still have to check it, and you still need to know your way around Figma properly.My prompt for this step, roughly as I say it:I want an exact mirror of this repo in Figma. The MCP is on and the file is empty. Let’s do this step by step. Transfer the tokens first. Always use the same naming as the code, so Figma and the code match. Set up collections that match the code, primitives and semantic. Alias them. Scope them. Where needed use modes (e.g. light and dark mode). Do the same for the text styles, using the naming from code, and use variables as in the code. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always. Then stop and tell me if you need anything.You will need to adapt this to your setup; mine is React with tokens in JSON, two layers. Once done, check in Figma that everything is set up correctly and compare with Storybook (I ask it to display all of this on a page for me).5. Build two components as a testNot the whole system. Two, ideally one simple and one awkward. I use Button and Alert, or some sort of dropdown; it’s fun with Figma.Now build the Alert and the Button component as a test, set up as in code, using my variables and styles. Anything you cannot express, write into GAPS.md always (GAPS.md I explain below; it’s the best part!).Then I go and look properly: are the variants complete, are the properties named as in code, is auto layout set up, are the tokens bound and scoped, did it carry the description across.That last part is where the real value sits. The two sides do not only look alike, they carry the same names and the same properties, down to the spelling. No danger on one side and error on the other, no Card that is secretly a Panel. Everything that comes later in an AI workflow stands on that: prototyping with real components, checking for drift, sending a screen back to code.If the two come out right, I run the whole library. And yes, that costs time and tokens. However, only once. Staying in sync afterwards is a different job: a contract, or in my case a parity check comparing two JSON lists. More on that soon.6. Know what you need! Context travels with each element, like a little parcelYou might have heard that context is key when working with AI design systems, especially later as we want to prototype with all of this stuff. Most of what gets called context is a markdown file: a DESIGN.md, a rules file, a page of guidelines. But most of the context is baked into the things themselves. Every token, every component, every style: think of each one as a little parcel carrying its own context.What is in the parcel:the component name, identical on both sideseach property with its allowed values and its defaulteach token name, what it points at, and where it is allowed to be used at allthe description written once in code and carried into the Figma componentthe code syntax on a Figma variable, so the variable knows what it is called in CSSa link back to that component’s page in Storybookand the gaps file, for everything that could not make the tripNone of that was typed into a document by hand, and to be honest, by hand I wouldn’t even get close. Markdown is for the why and the when, the rules and the exceptions. Everything factual gets generated and attached, and then it cannot quietly disagree with the code. Oh, how I love my MCP!7. Ask for the gaps, every single time via GAPS.mdYou might have noticed that I ask for GAPS.md every single time. I ended up with this one by accident. I wanted to know what had happened to all the things Figma could not express, so I asked the AI to list them, and the list turned out to be more useful than the components it had just built.Write a GAPS.md: everything you could not express in Figma, everything you were unsure about, and anything I should check by hand.The gaps exist whether or not anyone writes them down, and written down they become reviewable. My own gaps file contains things like line heights that are unitless in code and have to become pixels in Figma, states that only exist in behaviour, and layout rules Figma has no equivalent for. Each one with a note on what I decided. I also include a list of items the AI was unsure about that need my revision.A gaps file turns the imperfect mirror into a list you can take to a developer and work through, and you might come up with more creative ideas on how to use it.8. Turn what you learned into a skillBy the third run you will notice you are typing the same corrections. That is the moment to make a skill: a packaged set of instructions your AI loads automatically for this kind of job.Mine creates tokens and components, writes the gaps file, expects Storybook, then screenshots each generated component and compares it against the matching Storybook story, and compares manifests (a check I use later for parity). It exists because of my own mistakes, and I update it most weeks.One safety note, because I am asked this every time: a skill can run code on your machine. Make your own as a team or install them, but only from people you trust; read them, or have a developer look first or at least ask Claude to run through it before installing. Installing a random skill because it sounded handy is the same move as opening the “you have won a million” attachment.Keeping code and Figma parityGenerating the library once is the easy part. Keeping it true as the code changes week after week is the open problem, in my setup and in the industry generally.So I built myself a little parity checker and keep it as a status page inside Storybook; you can check it out here on my sync status page. You don’t need a page; you need a check, but I am a designer, so I need to see things visually.How it works, in three steps, quite unspectacular:Storybook can automatically write a component list. If you are using the Storybook MCP, it generates a file (JSON) called a manifest: every component, its properties, the allowed values and the defaults, straight out of the code. I only found it because of prototyping, where that short list is what makes AI prototyping work at all, since the agent reads the list instead of your whole repo. Which, by the way, is what got me into this whole setup in the first place, as I was so frustrated with the code output of AI builders when prototyping.So I asked Figma for the same thing. With the MCP open, I had Claude write me a matching list of what is really in my library: same components, same properties, same values. You can see the Figma JSON file I use here.Then I ran the two against each other. Name against name, property against property, default against default. Everything that matches turns green, anything that moved turns red. Easy!Both lists are JSON, which is just a text file where every value has a label, so a machine can compare them without interpreting anything.That comparison is deterministic, and that is exactly what we want: same input, same answer, every time, with no AI in it. The AI only kicks it off in my setup. The downside of mine is that I still have to trigger it by hand, and a real team would have a more sophisticated setup that runs automatically on every change. But very few teams have that right now.However, building it taught me more than reading about it ever did. I now have a much better idea of what my developers mean when they talk about checks, and I can sit in that conversation and help shape the workflow with design needs in mind.Side note: Right now it only checks the architecture, the names, properties, allowed values, and defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am working on that. Another side note: I initially called this a contract, but it isn’t. A contract sits above both sides and both get built from it. Mine compares two sides, and code wins every time, so the honest name is a parity check.“But I already have a Figma library. Can I update it with MCP? ”Most teams have one, often with years of work in it. The same connection can compare instead of create.I take a component I know is out of step, and I ask:In my open Figma file there is an Alert. Check it against the Alert in the code. This is a library file, so instances depend on it. Think it through with me: would a change list next to it be best, or should you generate a reference version from code next to it so I can compare, or do you want to propose a direct fix? Tell me here in the chat and add this as a visual note in Figma next to the component.What comes back is usually a report plus a clean reference component sitting next to the old one, which is a very calm way to have an argument with your own library (and yes, I renamed my component to Pizza just to show you a fail):The whole check runs through the MCP, and the answer is generated straight onto the canvas, next to the component it is about.Three warnings:Work on a copy. Never let an agent loose in a live library that other people’s files depend on. Duplicate first, test the workflow, then decide as a team.Deleted variants do not come back. Every variant has a key underneath its name. Delete it and rebuild it identically, and the instances out in the wild still will not reconnect. Rename and repair, do not delete and recreate.It still needs babysitting. On a real system with real history, this is assisted work, not magic. Go component by component, because the AI is quick and tireless and has no idea which differences matter. Once you are done, you can put a deterministic contract or other parity check on top that just checks whether things stay synced.I use this technique for any sort of check, e.g. accessibilityOnce you are aligned, you can do so much! Here’s an example: accessibility checks run in code, and then I get a little note like the one above in my Figma file next to the area with the issue and suggested solutions to discuss. Love it!This is what becomes possible once Figma and code hold the same tokens and structure: Contrast measured against the real tokens, then laid out in Figma through the MCPWhat if your product has more than one source?Everything above assumes one. My sample is one design system in code and Figma on top, so that code wins and there is nothing to argue about. With two it still holds: pick one as the source, mirror it into Figma, keep the names matching on the other side. At three- iOS, Android and web- it falls apart, because each of them holds part of the truth and none of them is wrong.You will not be the one deciding how that gets solved, and it decides what your Figma file can be, so it is worth knowing which one you are living in.A library per platform. You do exactly what this article describes, once per platform. Each library mirrors its own codebase, like three small projects side by side. The drift then is not really between Figma and code any more, it moves into the structure: there is no single Button, there are three, and they slowly grow apart. That is the kind of thing a team ends up talking about as a whole, and it is good to see it coming.Shared tokens, separate components. The one I see most often. Colours and spacing come from one source and land everywhere, while each platform keeps its own components, which is correct rather than sloppy, since a sheet is not a modal. You can mirror that split in Figma: one library for the variables and text styles, shared by everyone, and a component library per platform on top of it. The tokens are then safe to rely on, the component names are not.One platform as the reference. Usually web. Then it is this article again, one mirrored library, and the others follow its names as far as they can. Worth knowing which platform that is, and if nobody can tell you, that is your answer.Components defined as data. The one I find most promising comes from Nathan Curtis, whose talk about this idea I saw at SmashingConf Amsterdam in 2026 and really resonated with me. Instead of the definition living inside one codebase, every component is written down as data: its options, its allowed values, its defaults, in a plain file that sits above all the platforms. He calls it a contract (I wrote a longer article about contracts), and a schema says what a contract can contain. React, iOS, Android and Figma are all built from it and checked against it, so none of them is the original, and your Figma file stops being downstream of somebody else’s codebase.Worth exploring, and not only for this. If you follow me a bit longer you will see JSON files and deterministic checks turning up everywhere, including in prototyping, which is where this way of thinking really pays off. So if you are working at that size, have a look at Curtis’s Spectacular (not a paid placement, as usual, just an honest recommendation), a Figma plugin and a command-line tool that read a component into schema-valid YAML or Markdown and render specs back into Figma.The question to take back to your team is not which tool. It is which of these four you already are, and who is keeping it true.What this does not solveIt needs a system worth mirroring. If the code is a mess, you get a beautifully generated mess. And the clean codebase you can happily generate from is rarer than any of us pretend. Mine behaves because it is a sample system I built myself. Real ones have two generations of components living side by side, props called type1, half the things undocumented, and a Storybook somebody set up in 2024 and stopped feeding. The honest version is that you do not need the whole system to be clean, only the component you are mirroring today, which is why I keep going one component at a time. And the first generated run is quite good at showing you exactly where the mess is. But yes it is work, a lot of work to get AI-ready.Staying in sync is the open problem, and it’s tricky. My check tells me when the two have drifted; it does not stop them drifting, and I still trigger it by hand and in a playground. The state of the rest: Figma’s Code Connect links a component to its code but does not check whether they still agree, and it is on the larger plans only. Design system teams with engineers are building their own comparisons, which is the most common serious answer at the moment. Contracts are the most interesting direction and still early, closer to a proof of concept than something you install. And Figma’s own Code Sources (which they demoed at Config India in October 2026), which would point to the real system, is very promising, but still in closed beta. So if you feel behind on this, you are not. Almost nobody is doing it properly yet.It only checks the structure. Names, properties, values, defaults. Not the visual side, no CSS. I am currently playing with this step; I will keep you updated. Contracts do not solve this either as far as I understand it: they can say which token a part must use, which catches most drift, and they cannot tell you whether the thing looks right when it renders. That is visual regression testing, a separate tool on the code side, and between Figma and code it is still me looking at two screenshots (the MCP compares them for me). There’s interesting work happening, but if I missed anything, let me know.Library updates are hidden in Figma. This one caught me out properly. The library can be perfectly in sync and every designer still has to accept the update inside their own working file, and Figma buries that away in a corner. So half a team can be designing with last month’s Button, and nobody notices even though your setup is as polished as it gets.It needs someone who can read both sides. Not write code. Read it, enough to notice when a translation went wrong. Still worth more right now than learning another tool.Above all, this is also a human factor. All of this needs a change in workflow and mindset, on both sides. Designers have to read a codebase and to ask for access in the first place, which is the harder part. Developers have to prepare the system so it can be read, with typed props, descriptions and a clean manifest, and then be open about sharing it and inviting design in, which is the bigger ask. Nobody changes job, and reading code is worth more to a designer right now than another tool.📖 Words in this article.In-System Design (my term): designing with the system’s real components, on whichever surface suits the question, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.Props: the options a component accepts in code, like variant or size. Figma calls them component properties.Token: a named design decision, likebackground-accent, instead of a raw colour value. Primitives are the raw values, semantic tokens give them meaning, and aliased means the semantic one points at the primitive.Scoped (Figma): a variable is only offered where it belongs, so a text colour cannot be applied to a background.Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code. The examples you click through in Storybook.Manifest: the component as a list. Every prop, value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, from version 10 with the components manifest switched on.JSON: a plain text file where every value has a label, so a machine can read it without interpreting anything.MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it. Figma Console MCP (by Southleft) is the one I use for variables and library work.GAPS.md (my term): a file where the AI writes down everything it could not express, was unsure about, or faked.Skill: a packaged set of instructions an AI loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.Deterministic check: a comparison with no AI in it. Same input, same answer, every time.Parity check (what mine is): a deterministic comparison of two lists, code and Figma, where code wins.Drift: when the design and the code slowly stop matching, one small difference at a time.Component contract (Nathan Curtis and others): a component’s definition held as data, above any one platform, that code and Figma are both built from and checked against.Schema: the model that says what a contract is allowed to express.Code Connect (Figma): links a Figma component to its code so developers see the right snippet. It links, it does not check, and it is on the larger plans.Visual regression testing: screenshots of the real rendered components, compared automatically on every change, so anything that shifts shows up as a difference.Variant key (Figma): the invisible id under a variant’s name. Delete the variant and the key goes with it, which is why rebuilt variants do not reconnect to instances.In-System Design: a three-part series.Part 1: Building an AI-ready design system: Code → Figma (you are here)Part 2: AI prototyping inside your design system (3 November 2026)Part 3: From code to Figma and back (10 November 2026)About the author: Christine VallaureI’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.Currently, I offer these formats in these formats:Build Scalable UI in Figma & AI: Design Systems Agents Can Actually Use · four-week, full Figma from the ground up, design system basics, and AI topics like these on top.AI Design Systems & Prototyping for Designers · a two-week intensive that runs through exactly this workflow and the prototyping that follows it, for designers who already know their way around Figma and basic design system principles.In-house team training · my favourite part. item.title: Tesla (TSLA) proxy shows a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger
item.description: Tesla’s proxy for its 2026 annual meeting, filed today, confirms that one of its supposedly independent directors now sits on SpaceX’s board. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs both Tesla’s compensation committee and its governance committee, joined SpaceX’s board in February. That’s one of several details in the filing that line up with a Tesla-SpaceX merger. There’s a three-item ballot, an auto-voting program that kicks in for the next vote, and Musk pay terms that pay out on a deal price alone. more…
